I am not sure what the difference between “Internal-by-default with opt-in” and “Internal-by-default and public-by-default should both be possible, configurable per module” would be.

I voted for the latter one in order to make clear that Internal-by-default would need to be opt-in. The opt-in should be explicit, a solution like that proposed by PEP 842, where the use of a single export keyword somewhere in the whole module turns the default from everything-public to internal-by-default seams to be too implicit for me.

author: 25838728e19df16afdc5618d90b1905c01d9409fab1728c70c6e181d2ebe767e
html:
I replied as best as I could, but there were a lot of places where “I don’t understand the question” or “none of the above” were what I would have preferred. Rather than just answering “other” to everything, I made a best attempt. I hope that doesn’t distort the result too much, although there are certainly cases where you could implement what I voted for and I’d hate it…

The biggest issue for me is that it’s hard to answer in the absence of information on how we’d get to the final state. For example, I voted for access via a distinct interface, but a lot depends on what that interface is, and whether it’s designed to make accessing internals feel like you’re doing something wrong (as opposed to just making a choice on whether you’re comfortable with using something unsupported).

Internal by default is unacceptable to me if it affects existing modules, which weren’t designed with that in mind. But as a long term goal with a viable transition plan, it might be reasonable. I wasn’t able to choose it even if I wanted to, without more details.

As for declaration locality, my real answer is “alongside the documentation that explains what the public API is”. If that’s a module docstring, then “at the top” makes sense. If it’s function/class docstrings, “at point of definition” is best. If it’s in a separate document, neither is ideal and you’re in effect duplicating information. Whatever is easier to ensure docs and code are kept in sync applies then. So I said “both” - but randomly mixing the two approaches in the same module is (obviously, to me) a really bad idea, so the option I voted for (“can be mixed”) implies more freedom than I think is acceptable in practice.

Package level visibility is the one where I had the worst case of “I don’t understand the question”. I want to substitute “project” for “package”, but the two concepts aren’t quite the same and I don’t know how that would affect my answers. But taking “package” as the best we can do, it still depends. I’d want something like an “internal” pkg.utils module to be directly accessible everywhere in pkg, but I wouldn’t want private support functions in pkg.cli to be usable in pkg.networking, for example. And unit tests are a whole other issue - having to jump through extra hoops to access the internal support function that you’re specifically testing seems like unnecessary complexity. I said “same-package modules can directly access each other’s internals” because I think the status quo is the best we can realistically hope for here (especially if we are considering backward compatibility). And even that doesn’t cover tests, so I’d extend it to “same-package and test modules can directly access internals”.

One key thing that drives my views here. Within a single project, code as written now - with direct reference to internal names from anywhere within the project - is working code. It’s not wrong for a project to access its own internals. It may be a nasty bit of technical debt that the project would like to fix, but it’s not the same as an external user calling an API that’s not declared as public and supported. Therefore, in my view, backward compatibility requires that we don’t break this working code without the usual deprecation process. That means that (for example) the combination of “private by default” and “internals should be module level scoped” is not allowed without a deprecation and transition cycle under Python’s current backward compatibility policy.

This is where I get stuck with the whole “I don’t understand the question” problem. Options are being presented as if they are all equal, and the four questions are presented as independent. But they aren’t, once you take things like the compatibility policy into account. So as it stands, the poll is hiding (not intentionally, I’m sure!) a lot of important nuances around feasibility and complexity.

author: 9f760065eb7184f4a7aa54830b8a07fd27b3aed1df3b7f8cebded6656f29a6dd
html:
Paul Moore:

I replied as best as I could, but there were a lot of places where “I don’t understand the question” or “none of the above” were what I would have preferred. Rather than just answering “other” to everything, I made a best attempt.

Thanks for the detailed feedback.

As the previous discussions have shown the topic is complex with a lot of nuances and dependencies. So much that I got the impression that people partly talk past each other because of different mental models and unspoken assumptions; and also that discussions drift off into technical details of specific solutions, loosing the bigger picture of what we actually want or need.

The poll is an attempt to delineate key aspects to foster and guide further discussion. First by stating them as individual questions, and second by getting a high-level sentiment. Doing this is of course a strong simplification.

I acknowledge that the poll may feel vague and runs the danger of being too abstract, but not proposing concrete solutions yet is intentional. There can be different solutions to the same requirement. It’s not guaranteed that consensus on a solution can be reached or even that there is a technically feasible or justifiable (cost, compatibility, …) solution. - I’m deferring all the nitty gritty details to subsequent solution discussions.

The poll should rather serve as a muter or enhancer for follow-up discussions: If e.g. most people would say, they want to access internal and public symbols through the same interface, that discussion is done because that’s the status quo. If however, there is a strong interest in making access to internals different to access to public API, that’s only the starting point for figuring out details.

In that sense, yes please voter under a “best case” assumption: Vote for an entry if you see at least one appealing way of realizing it, and even if you think it’s generally a good idea worth discussing further, even if you are not sure whether it can be done or is worth it.

Paul Moore:

Options are being presented as if they are all equal, and the four questions are presented as independent. But they aren’t, once you take things like the compatibility policy into account. So as it stands, the poll is hiding (not intentionally, I’m sure!) a lot of important nuances around feasibility and complexity.

You are absolutely right with these observations. I’m aware of several nuances (though certainly not all). I’m not “hiding” them to gloss over issues and make people believe the world is simple. It’s not. Instead, leaving them out of the poll is intentional to be able to generate a coarse structured picture. It would not be possible to create a poll reflecting all the nuances and dependencies. The nuances will all resurface when we move back to discussing concrete solutions.

We’ll have to see whether something useful comes out of this approach.

html:
The scope is to me the most tricky one. I think importing from below should not have to use __internal__, though I guess that can be OK since a submodule can have everything public for modules above yet not have its contents exposed, if the submodule itself is not public.

But that leaves the example mentioned by Paul, of an pkg.utils module where you’d like to use its contents everywhere throughout pkg but not necessarily expose it to users who import from pkg. But perhaps even then from pkg.utils.__internal__ import ... actually states intent more clearly (… will change my vote a third time…)

Marten

author: 1358679b70dc53730c796772a915dd64534772340ca1a55831e92fe9ec0420b6
html:
I think authors will generally have many different views on what “internal” means, contrary to public.

Public is easy: it’s what I expose to users, and maintain to be free of breaking-changes.

Internal on the other hand can mean that the access at runtime is enforced or not, depending on a specific scope, whether bound to the language or how humans organize: same package, same module, same class, or same organization, same team, same project.

An example: you might want to completely prevent users from accessing an internal name, while allowing the same org uncomfortable access with a static analysis and runtime warning, while allowing the same team comfortable access with only a static analysis warning, while allowing the same project complete access without any warning. Or maybe something even finer grained, with package, module and class scopes.

What I mean is that maybe we should only standardize the public vs. internal declaration here (emphasis on public), and leave out what exactly “internal” means and implies. We’d drop questions 1 and 4.

The other option is of course to gather data around how projects handle and would like to handle internal APIs, and specify that too. But IMO there’s a clear cut and this can be done later.

html:
What I want:
Everything is public. Everything is accessible.

If an utility function is useful to the library author you can bet it will be useful to the user. Same thing with attributes.

It helps with learning (by exploration), it helps with tinkering.

How many times I had to fight with C++ or Java because public/private got in the way. There has never been a time where public/private was useful to me.

Please don’t import this to Python.

Having the possibility to document what is intended API and what to use at your own risk is fine.

focus solely on defining the mechanism to distinguish between public and internal, dropping aspects relevant to internal APIs only.

So what distinguishing behaviour would you expect of something that’s considered “public”, if you intend to leave internal names behaving as now? As far as I can see, you’d be left with public being just an annotation on certain names, with no distinct runtime behaviour at all.

Which, to be clear, I’m perfectly fine with - I’m happy with leaving the public/private distinction as a matter of documentation (and something tools flagh for the user). But others might not be.

Michael H:

This probably would have been a good place to use ranked choice voting.

Perhaps, but as I mentioned elsewhere, features don’t get added to Python by a DPO vote. Polls like this are useful to PEP authors to get a sense of where their proposals might have gaps or YAGNI, but ultimately I write the PEP for what I want and let the SC have the final say, which often includes suggested or required modifications.

That all said, thanks for putting this poll together @timhoffm

author: 26579313c0b390d4b23fa84f009af82eb70ab2c53970662141c46400f57c4fcc
html:
A lot of my preference hinges on what happens to the existing methods. I’m quite sympathetic to wanting something better than import sys as _sys for single file modules.

But I also think the status quo for packages or using underscore-prefixed submoules and an __init__.py to export the public stuff trumps all these proposals, anything involving __all__, and anything I’ve used in other languages.

So anything that breaks that or even just insinuates that __all__ (or whatever else we come up with) is the preferred/official/correct/modern way to publicise an API gets an automatic -1 from me.

And yet, people can like one and hate the other - so how do we interpret their vote?

We interpret the vote only to the degree it is designed for: High-level approaches, not concrete solutions. Please do not expect that a handful of questions can cover the whole soution space for a topic as complex an nuanced as pubilc/internal. The poll does not aim to settle on a solution, it only structures and narrows the solution space. This limitation is intentional - It’s not a bug, it’s a feature.

We still can learn a lot:

Interpretation:
People do not want a global declatation (which the current__all__ pattern is).
Learning 1: There is a need beyond the status quo, so it’s worth to go into the topic.

Note that somewhere in the PEP 844 discussion there were voices advocating that having a single place at the top of the file declaring the public interface is actually benificial. That’s apparently a minority.
Learning 2: While being logically sound, the single place argument is not what people care about.
Learning 3: Concerning PEP 844, the local definition is a fundamentally desired property. It’s not just an incidental byproduct of improving management of __all__

We have now established that a local definition is desirable. Whether that is best realized through a decorator, a keyword, or a naming convention is left to a followup discussion. It may even be that stating the general requirement “local definition” sparks additional solution ideas.

author: e27a87eeed8d855855de38d3a3c16c3132984b80e6c50bca7824c454c6d50380
html:
While I agree that the poll is somewhat confusing, I’m in favor of the broader goal of figuring out what we want before getting into the weeds of individual PEPs. There are now three PEPs on this just in the span of a few weeks, and there is a good bit of crosstalk in the discussions comparing them to one another, and in a fair number of cases it appears that at least some people are rejecting fundamental goals or assumptions of one or more of them[1]. It seems to me that it would be better to hash out some of the underlying issues to hopefully come up with a proposal that has the broadest support, rather than just choosing among the existing proposals.

If I were going to make a poll it might be more like a yes/no (or in some cases multiple choice) thing on each of several questions, like (this is just off the top of my head):

  1. Should anything be changed from the status quo (aka “is there any problem that needs to be solved”)?
  2. Should Python gain a mechanism to in any way modify or enforce access control of things in modules/packages?
    a. If so, do we need more than two levels of access (i.e., is it enough to have just “public/private” or do we need something like “public only to other modules within the same package”)?
  3. Should Python gain a way to explicitly specify in a structured/machine-readable way what “the public API” of a module/package is, so that tools like IDEs can read this info?
  4. Whatever it is you think Python needs, is it sufficiently important to warrant adding some notes to the docs/a builtin function/a soft keyword/a hard keyword?

I get the impression there is substantial disagreement even on these basic issues, and in that situation I think it’s best to make no changes for the moment, and see if we can come up with something that has more support.

  1. e.g., disagreements about whether any change should be purely advisory/documentary or should have some effect on the semantics of imports or attribute access ↩︎

author: cec2e6f882a95ba29228c9c77d595f2e847ab3fa6a8152ed0c67b45df8d25209
html:
Brendan Barnwell:
  1. Should anything be changed from the status quo (aka “is there any problem that needs to be solved”)?

Going beyond that, actually, what would be the problems to be solved?
My impression is that there is a sufficient weight of people who want particular problems with public/private solved, but that there is no particular problem that enough people care about.

I care about the specific problem that imports are formally part of the public API.
But how many people care about that problem? And is there a compromise solution that would make all the different people who care about different problems happy?

To me a sufficient combination of access control + machine readable public API is

git mv foo.py _foo.py

# foo.py
from _foo export (
  PublicSymbol1,
  PublicSymbol2,
  CONSTANT,
  ...
)

where the role of using export instead of import is to formally declare that these symbols are the public API.

Your tests can now test the public API and also test the internals. Users can use the internals, but only if they explicitly opt-in by importing from _ names.

But is that good enough for people who maintain large libraries? I don’t know.

Going beyond that, we may even need to concisely summarize the status quo first so that we have a shared full understanding, which may help pinning down the problems.

Relevant docs:

  1. 9. Classes — Python 3.14.7 documentation - defines single.leading-underscore semantics (in the context of classes, but also applying this to functions). It also defines double underscore name mangling
  2. 7. Simple statements — Python 3.14.7 documentation The import docs define what public names
  3. Distributing type information — typing documentation Typing docs

Some remarks:

  • Terminology is a bit sloppy. There is

    • private
    • “private”
    • class-private
    • non-public

    in particular private is used with variing meaning. Exactly defining the terms may help preventing misunderstands.

  • 2 and 3 have conflicting statements on whether imported symbols are public; see PEP 843: Export Statement for DRY Re-exports - #33 by timhoffm

  • The summary should also include patterns such as hub-and-spoke or import x as _x which build on the language convention but are not part of the docs.

author: 25838728e19df16afdc5618d90b1905c01d9409fab1728c70c6e181d2ebe767e
html:
Arguably, the status quo is “consenting adults”:

  • Authors make their intent as clear as they can (via whatever means they choose) and assume that consumers will respect that intent.
  • Consumers follow author’s wishes, and take responsibility for dealing with the consequences if they use features of the code that the author doesn’t offer support for.

Everything else (naming conventions, documentation, project layout) is basically just ways for people to communicate intent.

Of course that’s not particularly useful in a practical sense, but it does highlight one aspect of this discussion - namely that a lot of the mechanisms and formalisations people want to apply boil down to “how do I deal with consumers who won’t respect my intent?” And that’s a social problem rather than a technical one.

There’s another, less divisive, aspect, which is “how do I communicate my intent better if I need to?” Maybe that’s the one we should focus on…

author: 9f760065eb7184f4a7aa54830b8a07fd27b3aed1df3b7f8cebded6656f29a6dd
html:
Paul Moore:

There’s another, less divisive, aspect, which is “how do I communicate my intent better if I need to?” Maybe that’s the one we should focus on…

That is indeed the main question, but I’m afraid opinions are still quite diverse. Communication can involve documentation, conventions or language features. The language as an authoritative instance should define the ways how that communication should happen, so that library authors and users have a shared interpretation. In particular it has the aspects: (i) which intent can be communicated (e.g. is there a distinction between module-internal and package-internal); (ii) how can an author state their intent; (iii) how can a user read the intent and should there be measures to prevent accidental violations of intent.

author: 25838728e19df16afdc5618d90b1905c01d9409fab1728c70c6e181d2ebe767e
html:
Tim Hoffmann:

That is indeed the main question, but I’m afraid opinions are still quite diverse.

Agreed.

My intent is pretty simple: These are the names/features/APIs I consider to be public and supported, use them freely and if anything doesn’t behave as documented feel free to let me know and I’ll see what I can do[1]. Anything else is private, and while you can still use them freely, it’s your responsibility if you do, and don’t expect me to care if something goes wrong.

As long as I can continue to take that stance, I don’t care that much. Features that make it easier (in my opinion) for me to express my intent, or for my users to discover my intent, are welcome - on the assumption that if I don’t want to use those features, nothing forces me to do so.

Language level statements on how I “must” state my intent, or how my users “must” interact with my code, are not acceptable to me. Similarly, social-level pronouncements on best practices (such as “everyone should use hubs”) are not acceptable - it’s unfortunate but true that “best practice zealots” tend to force their views on others, whether by social pressure, on-by-default linter rules, or some other means.

Essentially, backward compatibility rules here - don’t break working code (not even by PEP 8 style “guidelines”).

That’s why I’m against compatibility-breaking changes like “private by default”, or approaches that make adopting useful new ways of expressing intent have knock-on breaking effects like “accessing private names requires a special mechanism”[2].

  1. Within the limits of the fact that I’m a volunteer and I don’t have to do anything… ↩︎

  2. This latter case boils down to “you can’t adopt this feature for expressing intent unless you accept our preferred enforcement policy” ↩︎

author: 9f760065eb7184f4a7aa54830b8a07fd27b3aed1df3b7f8cebded6656f29a6dd
html:
Paul Moore:

Essentially, backward compatibility rules here - don’t break working code (not even by PEP 8 style “guidelines”).

Absolutely agree. Neither me nor anybody with a bit of experience with widely used software would introduce backward incomatible changes unless there are very very compelling reasons (and then only with a migration strategy).

Paul Moore:

That’s why I’m against compatibility-breaking changes like “private by default”

I suspect there’s one or two misunderstandings here, and I’m taking the responsibility that the poll questions may not be written clear enough or are lacking context.
First do we agree that “private” here is “internal” or “non-public”? It has nothing to do with making things inaccessible (I avoid the term “private” because in other languages it often has the connotation of inaccessible).
Second “internal by default” means: “I as an author would like to mark the public parts of my API, everything else is considered internal.” - as opposed to “I would like to mark the internal symbols - everything else is considered public”. When nothing else is given Python is public-by-default (everything is public and you mark internal names by a leading underscore). The __all__ mechanism makes a module internal-by-default (only the listed names are public, everything else is internal). There’s no breaking change involved because defining __all__ is an explicit opt-in decision of the author.
Likewise any other reasonable way of specifying the public/internal names would be opt-in and non-breaking.

author: 759f04163031c8f80f61bd5c2361c3d0172f137eafcd1387855dc724906d4eb8
html:
First off, I would like to apologize for the chaos caused by PEP 842. When I first wrote it, I definitely did not envision several separate proposals arising from it – I applaud everyone who has poured time and effort into these discussions!

Now, having read all of these, I’m convinced of the following:

  1. No runtime enforcement. We need a better way to express intent. At this point, I don’t think it’s worth the effort to try to stop people from deliberately accessing internals, and that wasn’t really my motivation for writing PEP 842 anyway. Libraries can ask for linter-level enforcement through a pyproject.toml entry or something.
  2. Anything that affects “intent” should affect dir(), help(), and IDE autocomplete, as those are all commonly used as quick ways to find things.
  3. Libraries want this for classes too, not just module-level names. No runtime enforcement makes this much simpler.

So, here’s a quick proposal for a sequel to the module exports trilogy: hidden and visible markers. Something like this:

# For now, I'm explicitly marking everything to avoid the need
# to choose a default behavior.
visible class Test:
    hidden def _internal():
        ...

    visible def public():
        self._internal()

hidden _INTERNAL_CONSTANT = 42
visible PUBLIC_CONSTANT = 24

It could also be a decorator + a type annotation, somewhat similar to PEP 844. The exact spelling isn’t important yet.

@visible
class Test:
    @hidden
    def _internal():
        ...

    @visible
    def public():
        ...

_INTERNAL_CONSTANT: hidden[int] = 42
PUBLIC_CONSTANT: public[int] = 24

Following in the footsteps of “type hints”, let’s call these “visibility hints”, since they don’t have any noticeable runtime effects (beyond dir, but that’s for introspection). This is a half-baked idea, but I’d be much more interested in pursuing something like this over the endless bickering about public/private. If anything, these threads have made it crystal clear that projects and developers have vastly different ideas about what “internal” means and how it should look in Python. I think we should just provide the infrastructure and let users choose how/whether they want to use it.

html:
I realize this may be the minority view here, but I think there’s also a strong case for valuing uniformity and simplicity.

A single, predictable rule for what counts as public or private has value in itself: it’s easier to explain, easier for users to reason about, and easier for tools to implement consistently. Preserving every historical behaviour can avoid short-term breakage, but it can also leave a language carrying increasingly complicated rules indefinitely.

C and C++ are probably an extreme example of the tradeoff: their strong commitment to backwards compatibility is really valuable for existing codebases, but it has also contributed to a huge amount of accumulated complexity.

I don’t think Python should casually break working code, but I also wouldn’t want “never break existing behaviour” to become an absolute principle if the alternative is a substantially simpler and more uniform model in the long run.

I also think there’s a difference between imposing a convention and recognizing one that has already developed organically. The underscore convention for private module- and class-level names is already overwhelmingly common, which is precisely why linters and other tools understand it by default. At some point, having the ecosystem converge on a convention makes Python easier to read and reason about across codebases.

A default linter rule isn’t the same thing as a language restriction: projects that disagree can disable it, while projects that follow the prevailing convention get useful behaviour without additional configuration. That seems to me like a healthy way for conventions to become standardized.

So anything that breaks that or even just insinuates that __all__ (or whatever else we come up with) is the preferred/official/correct/modern way to publicise an API gets an automatic -1 from me.

Why do you feel this is insinuation? The paragraph in the linked documentation paragraph reads pretty clear to me. I can however agree that it’s far from visible enough regarding the “public API” topic (is there even such a topic in the docs?).

Paul Moore:

So what distinguishing behaviour would you expect of something that’s considered “public”, if you intend to leave internal names behaving as now? As far as I can see, you’d be left with public being just an annotation on certain names, with no distinct runtime behaviour at all.

Yes, I would expect some kind of annotation (decorator, keyword, annotation metadata, etc.) that tells a name is public. If no such annotation is found within a module, then defaults apply (underscored names are private, etc.). I personally don’t care if this mechanism also somehow populates __all__, because I never use wildcard imports. But if we consider that __all__ is primarily used for declaring the public API, and that wildcard imports are a secondary concern, then I’d argue that yes, __all__ should also be populated through this mechanism.

A nice consequence of PEP 843/844 or any work that hides __all__ under a new mechanism, is that we don’t have to manipulate __all__ directly anymore, meaning we can at some point change its semantics and/or documentation if we want to (for example rename it and create new __wildcard__, __exports__ or whatever dunder variables that make more sense) since it truly becomes an implementation detail.

author: 4e77df27ac996b56fe0bfea8d789205c72b3808442c0d8af9fd84cb05e9827a5
html:
Tim Hoffmann:

Please answer based on the behavior you would prefer, rather than on what you think is easiest to implement.

I think I’d personally prefer something along these lines:

from foo import_ bar

where import_ would mean: inside this module the name is simply bar, but from outside the module it is exposed as _bar.

In other words:

# inside the module
bar(...)

but:

# from outside
module._bar

The main reason I’d want this is actually quite mundane: less typing when importing implementation details. I find from foo import bar as _bar a little unfortunate because the underscore then propagates through all uses of the name inside the module.

For my own libraries, I think this would be enough that I’d probably never use __all__: the leading-underscore convention already covers all of my use cases. I prefer the visibility decision to live at the import/definition site rather than maintaining a separate list that can get out of sync.

I’m not suggesting this as a concrete proposal for the current discussion so much as pointing out a behavior/syntax I’d personally find useful: private to consumers, but without requiring the private spelling inside the implementation.

html:
Following the recent discussions around PEP 842, PEP 843, and PEP 844, and using two namespaces, I’d like to get a broader sense of what semantics people actually want from a public/internal distinction.

The goal of this poll is to understand what behavior people would find most useful, not to choose a particular syntax or implementation.

Please answer based on the behavior you would prefer, rather than on what you think is easiest to implement.

Access to internal names: How should code outside a module access its internal symbols?
  • Through the same interface as public symbols, e.g. module.internal_name (current approach)
  • Through a distinct interface, e.g. module.__internal__.internal_name
  • Internal symbols should not be externally accessible
  • No preference
  • Other
0 voters
Default visibility: Should names (e.g. declared functions) be
  • Internal-by-default, with public names explicitly marked
  • Public-by-default, with internal names explicitly marked
  • Neither: every name explicitly classified
  • Internal-by-default and public-by-default should both be possible, configurable per module
  • No preference
  • Other
0 voters
Declaration locality: Where/how should the public/internal distinction be declared?
  • Centrally at the top of the module
  • Locally next to the definitions
  • Configurable per module
  • Both central and local declarations can be mixed
  • No preference
  • Other
0 voters
Package-level visibility: Should modules in the same package get direct access to each other’s internals?
  • Yes, same-package modules can directly access each other’s internals
  • No, internals should be module-level scoped. Other same-package modules will need to go through the same opt-in mechanism for internal access just like any other external code
  • Introduce a separate package-internal visibility level, distinct from public and module-internal
  • No preference
  • Other
0 voters

Propsals for different behavior and why you chose “Other” as an answer are welcome below. Please refrain from going into discussing concrete solutions and implementation aspects. I’d like to keep this focussed on requirements engineering.

html:
You haven’t provided a “The way things are right now.” option for anything, but based on the solutions so far I don’t really see them helping with any problem I have and they’re all more complex than the status quo, so I don’t particularly want any of them.

Type checkers already work well enough for the level of visibility being discussed. As a library author, I need to be able to define the public API, without affecting runtime access to it, at both the module and class level, and I want that to be a single consistent solution.

The status quo is:

  • Access to external names: directly, regardless of if they’re marked public/private somehow.
  • Default visibility: public if not _ prefixed name, or public if in __all__ if __all__ is defined, or public if re-xported import name as name.
  • Declaration locality: _ prefixed name, or __all__ somewhere, or import name as name somewhere.
  • Package-level visibility: same as first question: direct access, regardless of public/private mark

html:
This probably would have been a good place to use ranked choice voting. There’s also several details that I consider important to which behavior I’d prefer in some cases, and it can’t be seperated.

I prefer at top of module declaration if it has to be managed. I don’t find keeping __all__ up to date hard, it’s not a common action to add something to the public API of a module, and you should know when you do it. A single extra thing that might need updating when adding something new to a module is not a large burden, and it’s simple.

I wouldn’t want to use a decorator to “manage this for me”, unless it did something more than just add it to some export list, like add a message users would get on attempting to access something private, but I also think private should be the default for modules, so that’s a tiny side-concern if private by default happens.

However, if we are getting syntax for this, then that calculus shifts a bit. Depending on the specifics of the syntax (are the names chosen appropriately extendible to classes in the future?) I would expect it to be in-line for consistent application.

I think you’re trying to condense too much of the discussion into a set of polls here, so I hope anywhere you take it after this doesn’t leave out any of the nuance that these polls do.

However, if we are getting syntax for this, then that calculus shifts a bit. Depending on the specifics of the syntax (are the names chosen appropriately extendible to classes in the future?) I would expect it to be in-line for consistent application. I think you’re trying to condense too much of the discussion into a set of polls here, so I hope anywhere you take it after this doesn’t leave out any of the nuance that these polls do.

author: 25838728e19df16afdc5618d90b1905c01d9409fab1728c70c6e181d2ebe767e
html:
I replied as best as I could, but there were a lot of places where “I don’t understand the question” or “none of the above” were what I would have preferred. Rather than just answering “other” to everything, I made a best attempt. I hope that doesn’t distort the result too much, although there are certainly cases where you could implement what I voted for and I’d hate it…

The biggest issue for me is that it’s hard to answer in the absence of information on how we’d get to the final state. For example, I voted for access via a distinct interface, but a lot depends on what that interface is, and whether it’s designed to make accessing internals feel like you’re doing something wrong (as opposed to just making a choice on whether you’re comfortable with using something unsupported).

Internal by default is unacceptable to me if it affects existing modules, which weren’t designed with that in mind. But as a long term goal with a viable transition plan, it might be reasonable. I wasn’t able to choose it even if I wanted to, without more details.

As for declaration locality, my real answer is “alongside the documentation that explains what the public API is”. If that’s a module docstring, then “at the top” makes sense. If it’s function/class docstrings, “at point of definition” is best. If it’s in a separate document, neither is ideal and you’re in effect duplicating information. Whatever is easier to ensure docs and code are kept in sync applies then. So I said “both” - but randomly mixing the two approaches in the same module is (obviously, to me) a really bad idea, so the option I voted for (“can be mixed”) implies more freedom than I think is acceptable in practice.

Package level visibility is the one where I had the worst case of “I don’t understand the question”. I want to substitute “project” for “package”, but the two concepts aren’t quite the same and I don’t know how that would affect my answers. But taking “package” as the best we can do, it still depends. I’d want something like an “internal” pkg.utils module to be directly accessible everywhere in pkg, but I wouldn’t want private support functions in pkg.cli to be usable in pkg.networking, for example. And unit tests are a whole other issue - having to jump through extra hoops to access the internal support function that you’re specifically testing seems like unnecessary complexity. I said “same-package modules can directly access each other’s internals” because I think the status quo is the best we can realistically hope for here (especially if we are considering backward compatibility). And even that doesn’t cover tests, so I’d extend it to “same-package and test modules can directly access internals”.

One key thing that drives my views here. Within a single project, code as written now - with direct reference to internal names from anywhere within the project - is working code. It’s not wrong for a project to access its own internals. It may be a nasty bit of technical debt that the project would like to fix, but it’s not the same as an external user calling an API that’s not declared as public and supported. Therefore, in my view, backward compatibility requires that we don’t break this working code without the usual deprecation process. That means that (for example) the combination of “private by default” and “internals should be module level scoped” is not allowed without a deprecation and transition cycle under Python’s current backward compatibility policy.

This is where I get stuck with the whole “I don’t understand the question” problem. Options are being presented as if they are all equal, and the four questions are presented as independent. But they aren’t, once you take things like the compatibility policy into account. So as it stands, the poll is hiding (not intentionally, I’m sure!) a lot of important nuances around feasibility and complexity.

author: 9f760065eb7184f4a7aa54830b8a07fd27b3aed1df3b7f8cebded6656f29a6dd
html:
Paul Moore:

I replied as best as I could, but there were a lot of places where “I don’t understand the question” or “none of the above” were what I would have preferred. Rather than just answering “other” to everything, I made a best attempt.

Thanks for the detailed feedback.

As the previous discussions have shown the topic is complex with a lot of nuances and dependencies. So much that I got the impression that people partly talk past each other because of different mental models and unspoken assumptions; and also that discussions drift off into technical details of specific solutions, loosing the bigger picture of what we actually want or need.

The poll is an attempt to delineate key aspects to foster and guide further discussion. First by stating them as individual questions, and second by getting a high-level sentiment. Doing this is of course a strong simplification.

I acknowledge that the poll may feel vague and runs the danger of being too abstract, but not proposing concrete solutions yet is intentional. There can be different solutions to the same requirement. It’s not guaranteed that consensus on a solution can be reached or even that there is a technically feasible or justifiable (cost, compatibility, …) solution. - I’m deferring all the nitty gritty details to subsequent solution discussions.

The poll should rather serve as a muter or enhancer for follow-up discussions: If e.g. most people would say, they want to access internal and public symbols through the same interface, that discussion is done because that’s the status quo. If however, there is a strong interest in making access to internals different to access to public API, that’s only the starting point for figuring out details.

In that sense, yes please voter under a “best case” assumption: Vote for an entry if you see at least one appealing way of realizing it, and even if you think it’s generally a good idea worth discussing further, even if you are not sure whether it can be done or is worth it.

Paul Moore:

Options are being presented as if they are all equal, and the four questions are presented as independent. But they aren’t, once you take things like the compatibility policy into account. So as it stands, the poll is hiding (not intentionally, I’m sure!) a lot of important nuances around feasibility and complexity.

You are absolutely right with these observations. I’m aware of several nuances (though certainly not all). I’m not “hiding” them to gloss over issues and make people believe the world is simple. It’s not. Instead, leaving them out of the poll is intentional to be able to generate a coarse structured picture. It would not be possible to create a poll reflecting all the nuances and dependencies. The nuances will all resurface when we move back to discussing concrete solutions.

We’ll have to see whether something useful comes out of this approach.

author: 1358679b70dc53730c796772a915dd64534772340ca1a55831e92fe9ec0420b6
html:
I think authors will generally have many different views on what “internal” means, contrary to public.

Public is easy: it’s what I expose to users, and maintain to be free of breaking-changes.

Internal on the other hand can mean that the access at runtime is enforced or not, depending on a specific scope, whether bound to the language or how humans organize: same package, same module, same class, or same organization, same team, same project.

An example: you might want to completely prevent users from accessing an internal name, while allowing the same org uncomfortable access with a static analysis and runtime warning, while allowing the same team comfortable access with only a static analysis warning, while allowing the same project complete access without any warning. Or maybe something even finer grained, with package, module and class scopes.

What I mean is that maybe we should only standardize the public vs. internal declaration here (emphasis on public), and leave out what exactly “internal” means and implies. We’d drop questions 1 and 4.

The other option is of course to gather data around how projects handle and would like to handle internal APIs, and specify that too. But IMO there’s a clear cut and this can be done later.

Everything is public. Everything is accessible.

html:
A lot of my preference hinges on what happens to the existing methods. I’m quite sympathetic to wanting something better than import sys as _sys for single file modules.

But I also think the status quo for packages or using underscore-prefixed submoules and an __init__.py to export the public stuff trumps all these proposals, anything involving __all__, and anything I’ve used in other languages.

So anything that breaks that or even just insinuates that __all__ (or whatever else we come up with) is the preferred/official/correct/modern way to publicise an API gets an automatic -1 from me.

Declaring that a name is private by using an underscore is entirely in line with “public/internal should be declared locally next to the definition”. So is @public. And yet, people can like one and hate the other - so how do we interpret their vote?

We interpret the vote only to the degree it is designed for: High-level approaches, not concrete solutions. Please do not expect that a handful of questions can cover the whole soution space for a topic as complex an nuanced as pubilc/internal. The poll does not aim to settle on a solution, it only structures and narrows the solution space. This limitation is intentional - It’s not a bug, it’s a feature.

We still can learn a lot:

Interpretation:
People do not want a global declatation (which the current__all__ pattern is).
Learning 1: There is a need beyond the status quo, so it’s worth to go into the topic.

Note that somewhere in the PEP 844 discussion there were voices advocating that having a single place at the top of the file declaring the public interface is actually benificial. That’s apparently a minority.
Learning 2: While being logically sound, the single place argument is not what people care about.
Learning 3: Concerning PEP 844, the local definition is a fundamentally desired property. It’s not just an incidental byproduct of improving management of __all__

We have now established that a local definition is desirable. Whether that is best realized through a decorator, a keyword, or a naming convention is left to a followup discussion. It may even be that stating the general requirement “local definition” sparks additional solution ideas.

author: e27a87eeed8d855855de38d3a3c16c3132984b80e6c50bca7824c454c6d50380
html:
While I agree that the poll is somewhat confusing, I’m in favor of the broader goal of figuring out what we want before getting into the weeds of individual PEPs. There are now three PEPs on this just in the span of a few weeks, and there is a good bit of crosstalk in the discussions comparing them to one another, and in a fair number of cases it appears that at least some people are rejecting fundamental goals or assumptions of one or more of them[1]. It seems to me that it would be better to hash out some of the underlying issues to hopefully come up with a proposal that has the broadest support, rather than just choosing among the existing proposals.

If I were going to make a poll it might be more like a yes/no (or in some cases multiple choice) thing on each of several questions, like (this is just off the top of my head):

  1. Should anything be changed from the status quo (aka “is there any problem that needs to be solved”)?
  2. Should Python gain a mechanism to in any way modify or enforce access control of things in modules/packages?
    a. If so, do we need more than two levels of access (i.e., is it enough to have just “public/private” or do we need something like “public only to other modules within the same package”)?
  3. Should Python gain a way to explicitly specify in a structured/machine-readable way what “the public API” of a module/package is, so that tools like IDEs can read this info?
  4. Whatever it is you think Python needs, is it sufficiently important to warrant adding some notes to the docs/a builtin function/a soft keyword/a hard keyword?

I get the impression there is substantial disagreement even on these basic issues, and in that situation I think it’s best to make no changes for the moment, and see if we can come up with something that has more support.

  1. e.g., disagreements about whether any change should be purely advisory/documentary or should have some effect on the semantics of imports or attribute access ↩︎

author: cec2e6f882a95ba29228c9c77d595f2e847ab3fa6a8152ed0c67b45df8d25209
html:
Brendan Barnwell:
  1. Should anything be changed from the status quo (aka “is there any problem that needs to be solved”)?

Going beyond that, actually, what would be the problems to be solved?
My impression is that there is a sufficient weight of people who want particular problems with public/private solved, but that there is no particular problem that enough people care about.

I care about the specific problem that imports are formally part of the public API.
But how many people care about that problem? And is there a compromise solution that would make all the different people who care about different problems happy?

To me a sufficient combination of access control + machine readable public API is

git mv foo.py _foo.py

# foo.py
from _foo export (
  PublicSymbol1,
  PublicSymbol2,
  CONSTANT,
  ...
)

where the role of using export instead of import is to formally declare that these symbols are the public API.

Your tests can now test the public API and also test the internals. Users can use the internals, but only if they explicitly opt-in by importing from _ names.

But is that good enough for people who maintain large libraries? I don’t know.

html:
peter:

Going beyond that, actually, what would be the problems to be solved?

Going beyond that, we may even need to concisely summarize the status quo first so that we have a shared full understanding, which may help pinning down the problems.

Relevant docs:

  1. 9. Classes — Python 3.14.7 documentation - defines single.leading-underscore semantics (in the context of classes, but also applying this to functions). It also defines double underscore name mangling
  2. 7. Simple statements — Python 3.14.7 documentation The import docs define what public names
  3. Distributing type information — typing documentation Typing docs

Some remarks:

  • Terminology is a bit sloppy. There is

    • private
    • “private”
    • class-private
    • non-public

    in particular private is used with variing meaning. Exactly defining the terms may help preventing misunderstands.

  • 2 and 3 have conflicting statements on whether imported symbols are public; see PEP 843: Export Statement for DRY Re-exports - #33 by timhoffm

  • The summary should also include patterns such as hub-and-spoke or import x as _x which build on the language convention but are not part of the docs.

author: 25838728e19df16afdc5618d90b1905c01d9409fab1728c70c6e181d2ebe767e
html:
Arguably, the status quo is “consenting adults”:

  • Authors make their intent as clear as they can (via whatever means they choose) and assume that consumers will respect that intent.
  • Consumers follow author’s wishes, and take responsibility for dealing with the consequences if they use features of the code that the author doesn’t offer support for.

Everything else (naming conventions, documentation, project layout) is basically just ways for people to communicate intent.

Of course that’s not particularly useful in a practical sense, but it does highlight one aspect of this discussion - namely that a lot of the mechanisms and formalisations people want to apply boil down to “how do I deal with consumers who won’t respect my intent?” And that’s a social problem rather than a technical one.

There’s another, less divisive, aspect, which is “how do I communicate my intent better if I need to?” Maybe that’s the one we should focus on…

author: 9f760065eb7184f4a7aa54830b8a07fd27b3aed1df3b7f8cebded6656f29a6dd
html:
Paul Moore:

There’s another, less divisive, aspect, which is “how do I communicate my intent better if I need to?” Maybe that’s the one we should focus on…

That is indeed the main question, but I’m afraid opinions are still quite diverse. Communication can involve documentation, conventions or language features. The language as an authoritative instance should define the ways how that communication should happen, so that library authors and users have a shared interpretation. In particular it has the aspects: (i) which intent can be communicated (e.g. is there a distinction between module-internal and package-internal); (ii) how can an author state their intent; (iii) how can a user read the intent and should there be measures to prevent accidental violations of intent.

author: 25838728e19df16afdc5618d90b1905c01d9409fab1728c70c6e181d2ebe767e
html:
Tim Hoffmann:

That is indeed the main question, but I’m afraid opinions are still quite diverse.

Agreed.

My intent is pretty simple: These are the names/features/APIs I consider to be public and supported, use them freely and if anything doesn’t behave as documented feel free to let me know and I’ll see what I can do[1]. Anything else is private, and while you can still use them freely, it’s your responsibility if you do, and don’t expect me to care if something goes wrong.

As long as I can continue to take that stance, I don’t care that much. Features that make it easier (in my opinion) for me to express my intent, or for my users to discover my intent, are welcome - on the assumption that if I don’t want to use those features, nothing forces me to do so.

Language level statements on how I “must” state my intent, or how my users “must” interact with my code, are not acceptable to me. Similarly, social-level pronouncements on best practices (such as “everyone should use hubs”) are not acceptable - it’s unfortunate but true that “best practice zealots” tend to force their views on others, whether by social pressure, on-by-default linter rules, or some other means.

Essentially, backward compatibility rules here - don’t break working code (not even by PEP 8 style “guidelines”).

That’s why I’m against compatibility-breaking changes like “private by default”, or approaches that make adopting useful new ways of expressing intent have knock-on breaking effects like “accessing private names requires a special mechanism”[2].

  1. Within the limits of the fact that I’m a volunteer and I don’t have to do anything… ↩︎

  2. This latter case boils down to “you can’t adopt this feature for expressing intent unless you accept our preferred enforcement policy” ↩︎

author: 9f760065eb7184f4a7aa54830b8a07fd27b3aed1df3b7f8cebded6656f29a6dd
html:
Paul Moore:

Essentially, backward compatibility rules here - don’t break working code (not even by PEP 8 style “guidelines”).

Absolutely agree. Neither me nor anybody with a bit of experience with widely used software would introduce backward incomatible changes unless there are very very compelling reasons (and then only with a migration strategy).

Paul Moore:

That’s why I’m against compatibility-breaking changes like “private by default”

I suspect there’s one or two misunderstandings here, and I’m taking the responsibility that the poll questions may not be written clear enough or are lacking context.
First do we agree that “private” here is “internal” or “non-public”? It has nothing to do with making things inaccessible (I avoid the term “private” because in other languages it often has the connotation of inaccessible).
Second “internal by default” means: “I as an author would like to mark the public parts of my API, everything else is considered internal.” - as opposed to “I would like to mark the internal symbols - everything else is considered public”. When nothing else is given Python is public-by-default (everything is public and you mark internal names by a leading underscore). The __all__ mechanism makes a module internal-by-default (only the listed names are public, everything else is internal). There’s no breaking change involved because defining __all__ is an explicit opt-in decision of the author.
Likewise any other reasonable way of specifying the public/internal names would be opt-in and non-breaking.

author: 759f04163031c8f80f61bd5c2361c3d0172f137eafcd1387855dc724906d4eb8
html:
First off, I would like to apologize for the chaos caused by PEP 842. When I first wrote it, I definitely did not envision several separate proposals arising from it – I applaud everyone who has poured time and effort into these discussions!

Now, having read all of these, I’m convinced of the following:

  1. No runtime enforcement. We need a better way to express intent. At this point, I don’t think it’s worth the effort to try to stop people from deliberately accessing internals, and that wasn’t really my motivation for writing PEP 842 anyway. Libraries can ask for linter-level enforcement through a pyproject.toml entry or something.
  2. Anything that affects “intent” should affect dir(), help(), and IDE autocomplete, as those are all commonly used as quick ways to find things.
  3. Libraries want this for classes too, not just module-level names. No runtime enforcement makes this much simpler.

So, here’s a quick proposal for a sequel to the module exports trilogy: hidden and visible markers. Something like this:

# For now, I'm explicitly marking everything to avoid the need
# to choose a default behavior.
visible class Test:
    hidden def _internal():
        ...

    visible def public():
        self._internal()

hidden _INTERNAL_CONSTANT = 42
visible PUBLIC_CONSTANT = 24

It could also be a decorator + a type annotation, somewhat similar to PEP 844. The exact spelling isn’t important yet.

@visible
class Test:
    @hidden
    def _internal():
        ...

    @visible
    def public():
        ...

_INTERNAL_CONSTANT: hidden[int] = 42
PUBLIC_CONSTANT: public[int] = 24

Following in the footsteps of “type hints”, let’s call these “visibility hints”, since they don’t have any noticeable runtime effects (beyond dir, but that’s for introspection). This is a half-baked idea, but I’d be much more interested in pursuing something like this over the endless bickering about public/private. If anything, these threads have made it crystal clear that projects and developers have vastly different ideas about what “internal” means and how it should look in Python. I think we should just provide the infrastructure and let users choose how/whether they want to use it.

Something like this: # For now, I'm explicitly marking everything to avoid the need # to choose a default behavior. visible class Test: hidden def _internal(): ... visible def public(): self._internal() hidden _INTERNAL_CONSTANT = 42 visible PUBLIC_CONSTANT = 24 It could also be a decorator + a type annotation, somewhat similar to PEP 844. The exact spelling isn’t important yet. @visible class Test: @hidden def _internal(): ... @visible def public(): ... _INTERNAL_CONSTANT: hidden[int] = 42 PUBLIC_CONSTANT: public[int] = 24 Following in the footsteps of “type hints”, let’s call these “visibility hints”, since they don’t have any noticeable runtime effects (beyond dir , but that’s for introspection). This is a half-baked idea, but I’d be much more interested in pursuing something like this over the endless bickering about public/private. If anything, these threads have made it crystal clear that projects and developers have vastly different ideas about what “internal” means and how it should look in Python. I think we should just provide the infrastructure and let users choose how/whether they want to use it.

author: a91ba60ff544a77a75e30cd6b567108507bde1675528e5820d6aee41e60f83b4
html:
I realize this may be the minority view here, but I think there’s also a strong case for valuing uniformity and simplicity.

A single, predictable rule for what counts as public or private has value in itself: it’s easier to explain, easier for users to reason about, and easier for tools to implement consistently. Preserving every historical behaviour can avoid short-term breakage, but it can also leave a language carrying increasingly complicated rules indefinitely.

C and C++ are probably an extreme example of the tradeoff: their strong commitment to backwards compatibility is really valuable for existing codebases, but it has also contributed to a huge amount of accumulated complexity.

I don’t think Python should casually break working code, but I also wouldn’t want “never break existing behaviour” to become an absolute principle if the alternative is a substantially simpler and more uniform model in the long run.

I also think there’s a difference between imposing a convention and recognizing one that has already developed organically. The underscore convention for private module- and class-level names is already overwhelmingly common, which is precisely why linters and other tools understand it by default. At some point, having the ecosystem converge on a convention makes Python easier to read and reason about across codebases.

A default linter rule isn’t the same thing as a language restriction: projects that disagree can disable it, while projects that follow the prevailing convention get useful behaviour without additional configuration. That seems to me like a healthy way for conventions to become standardized.

So what distinguishing behaviour would you expect of something that’s considered “public”, if you intend to leave internal names behaving as now? As far as I can see, you’d be left with public being just an annotation on certain names, with no distinct runtime behaviour at all.

Yes, I would expect some kind of annotation (decorator, keyword, annotation metadata, etc.) that tells a name is public. I personally don’t care if this mechanism also somehow populates __all__, because I never use wildcard imports. author: 4e77df27ac996b56fe0bfea8d789205c72b3808442c0d8af9fd84cb05e9827a5
html:
Tim Hoffmann:

Please answer based on the behavior you would prefer, rather than on what you think is easiest to implement.

I think I’d personally prefer something along these lines:

from foo import_ bar

where import_ would mean: inside this module the name is simply bar, but from outside the module it is exposed as _bar.

In other words:

# inside the module
bar(...)

but:

# from outside
module._bar

The main reason I’d want this is actually quite mundane: less typing when importing implementation details. I find from foo import bar as _bar a little unfortunate because the underscore then propagates through all uses of the name inside the module.

For my own libraries, I think this would be enough that I’d probably never use __all__: the leading-underscore convention already covers all of my use cases. I prefer the visibility decision to live at the import/definition site rather than maintaining a separate list that can get out of sync.

I’m not suggesting this as a concrete proposal for the current discussion so much as pointing out a behavior/syntax I’d personally find useful: private to consumers, but without requiring the private spelling inside the implementation.

html:
Following the recent discussions around PEP 842, PEP 843, and PEP 844, and using two namespaces, I’d like to get a broader sense of what semantics people actually want from a public/internal distinction.

The goal of this poll is to understand what behavior people would find most useful, not to choose a particular syntax or implementation.

Please answer based on the behavior you would prefer, rather than on what you think is easiest to implement.

Access to internal names: How should code outside a module access its internal symbols?
  • Through the same interface as public symbols, e.g. module.internal_name (current approach)
  • Through a distinct interface, e.g. module.__internal__.internal_name
  • Internal symbols should not be externally accessible
  • No preference
  • Other
0 voters
Default visibility: Should names (e.g. declared functions) be
  • Internal-by-default, with public names explicitly marked
  • Public-by-default, with internal names explicitly marked
  • Neither: every name explicitly classified
  • Internal-by-default and public-by-default should both be possible, configurable per module
  • No preference
  • Other
0 voters
Declaration locality: Where/how should the public/internal distinction be declared?
  • Centrally at the top of the module
  • Locally next to the definitions
  • Configurable per module
  • Both central and local declarations can be mixed
  • No preference
  • Other
0 voters
Package-level visibility: Should modules in the same package get direct access to each other’s internals?
  • Yes, same-package modules can directly access each other’s internals
  • No, internals should be module-level scoped. Other same-package modules will need to go through the same opt-in mechanism for internal access just like any other external code
  • Introduce a separate package-internal visibility level, distinct from public and module-internal
  • No preference
  • Other
0 voters

Propsals for different behavior and why you chose “Other” as an answer are welcome below. Please refrain from going into discussing concrete solutions and implementation aspects. I’d like to keep this focussed on requirements engineering.

html:
You haven’t provided a “The way things are right now.” option for anything, but based on the solutions so far I don’t really see them helping with any problem I have and they’re all more complex than the status quo, so I don’t particularly want any of them.

Type checkers already work well enough for the level of visibility being discussed. As a library author, I need to be able to define the public API, without affecting runtime access to it, at both the module and class level, and I want that to be a single consistent solution.

The status quo is:

  • Access to external names: directly, regardless of if they’re marked public/private somehow.
  • Default visibility: public if not _ prefixed name, or public if in __all__ if __all__ is defined, or public if re-xported import name as name.
  • Declaration locality: _ prefixed name, or __all__ somewhere, or import name as name somewhere.
  • Package-level visibility: same as first question: direct access, regardless of public/private mark

html:
This probably would have been a good place to use ranked choice voting. There’s also several details that I consider important to which behavior I’d prefer in some cases, and it can’t be seperated.

I prefer at top of module declaration if it has to be managed. I don’t find keeping __all__ up to date hard, it’s not a common action to add something to the public API of a module, and you should know when you do it. A single extra thing that might need updating when adding something new to a module is not a large burden, and it’s simple.

I wouldn’t want to use a decorator to “manage this for me”, unless it did something more than just add it to some export list, like add a message users would get on attempting to access something private, but I also think private should be the default for modules, so that’s a tiny side-concern if private by default happens.

However, if we are getting syntax for this, then that calculus shifts a bit. Depending on the specifics of the syntax (are the names chosen appropriately extendible to classes in the future?) I would expect it to be in-line for consistent application.

I think you’re trying to condense too much of the discussion into a set of polls here, so I hope anywhere you take it after this doesn’t leave out any of the nuance that these polls do.

author: 25838728e19df16afdc5618d90b1905c01d9409fab1728c70c6e181d2ebe767e
html:
I replied as best as I could, but there were a lot of places where “I don’t understand the question” or “none of the above” were what I would have preferred. Rather than just answering “other” to everything, I made a best attempt. I hope that doesn’t distort the result too much, although there are certainly cases where you could implement what I voted for and I’d hate it…

The biggest issue for me is that it’s hard to answer in the absence of information on how we’d get to the final state. For example, I voted for access via a distinct interface, but a lot depends on what that interface is, and whether it’s designed to make accessing internals feel like you’re doing something wrong (as opposed to just making a choice on whether you’re comfortable with using something unsupported).

Internal by default is unacceptable to me if it affects existing modules, which weren’t designed with that in mind. But as a long term goal with a viable transition plan, it might be reasonable. I wasn’t able to choose it even if I wanted to, without more details.

As for declaration locality, my real answer is “alongside the documentation that explains what the public API is”. If that’s a module docstring, then “at the top” makes sense. If it’s function/class docstrings, “at point of definition” is best. If it’s in a separate document, neither is ideal and you’re in effect duplicating information. Whatever is easier to ensure docs and code are kept in sync applies then. So I said “both” - but randomly mixing the two approaches in the same module is (obviously, to me) a really bad idea, so the option I voted for (“can be mixed”) implies more freedom than I think is acceptable in practice.

Package level visibility is the one where I had the worst case of “I don’t understand the question”. I want to substitute “project” for “package”, but the two concepts aren’t quite the same and I don’t know how that would affect my answers. But taking “package” as the best we can do, it still depends. I’d want something like an “internal” pkg.utils module to be directly accessible everywhere in pkg, but I wouldn’t want private support functions in pkg.cli to be usable in pkg.networking, for example. And unit tests are a whole other issue - having to jump through extra hoops to access the internal support function that you’re specifically testing seems like unnecessary complexity. I said “same-package modules can directly access each other’s internals” because I think the status quo is the best we can realistically hope for here (especially if we are considering backward compatibility). And even that doesn’t cover tests, so I’d extend it to “same-package and test modules can directly access internals”.

One key thing that drives my views here. Within a single project, code as written now - with direct reference to internal names from anywhere within the project - is working code. It’s not wrong for a project to access its own internals. It may be a nasty bit of technical debt that the project would like to fix, but it’s not the same as an external user calling an API that’s not declared as public and supported. Therefore, in my view, backward compatibility requires that we don’t break this working code without the usual deprecation process. That means that (for example) the combination of “private by default” and “internals should be module level scoped” is not allowed without a deprecation and transition cycle under Python’s current backward compatibility policy.

This is where I get stuck with the whole “I don’t understand the question” problem. Options are being presented as if they are all equal, and the four questions are presented as independent. But they aren’t, once you take things like the compatibility policy into account. So as it stands, the poll is hiding (not intentionally, I’m sure!) a lot of important nuances around feasibility and complexity.

author: 9f760065eb7184f4a7aa54830b8a07fd27b3aed1df3b7f8cebded6656f29a6dd
html:
Paul Moore:

I replied as best as I could, but there were a lot of places where “I don’t understand the question” or “none of the above” were what I would have preferred. Rather than just answering “other” to everything, I made a best attempt.

Thanks for the detailed feedback.

As the previous discussions have shown the topic is complex with a lot of nuances and dependencies. So much that I got the impression that people partly talk past each other because of different mental models and unspoken assumptions; and also that discussions drift off into technical details of specific solutions, loosing the bigger picture of what we actually want or need.

The poll is an attempt to delineate key aspects to foster and guide further discussion. First by stating them as individual questions, and second by getting a high-level sentiment. Doing this is of course a strong simplification.

I acknowledge that the poll may feel vague and runs the danger of being too abstract, but not proposing concrete solutions yet is intentional. There can be different solutions to the same requirement. It’s not guaranteed that consensus on a solution can be reached or even that there is a technically feasible or justifiable (cost, compatibility, …) solution. - I’m deferring all the nitty gritty details to subsequent solution discussions.

The poll should rather serve as a muter or enhancer for follow-up discussions: If e.g. most people would say, they want to access internal and public symbols through the same interface, that discussion is done because that’s the status quo. If however, there is a strong interest in making access to internals different to access to public API, that’s only the starting point for figuring out details.

In that sense, yes please voter under a “best case” assumption: Vote for an entry if you see at least one appealing way of realizing it, and even if you think it’s generally a good idea worth discussing further, even if you are not sure whether it can be done or is worth it.

Paul Moore:

Options are being presented as if they are all equal, and the four questions are presented as independent. But they aren’t, once you take things like the compatibility policy into account. So as it stands, the poll is hiding (not intentionally, I’m sure!) a lot of important nuances around feasibility and complexity.

You are absolutely right with these observations. I’m aware of several nuances (though certainly not all). I’m not “hiding” them to gloss over issues and make people believe the world is simple. It’s not. Instead, leaving them out of the poll is intentional to be able to generate a coarse structured picture. It would not be possible to create a poll reflecting all the nuances and dependencies. The nuances will all resurface when we move back to discussing concrete solutions.

We’ll have to see whether something useful comes out of this approach.

author: 1358679b70dc53730c796772a915dd64534772340ca1a55831e92fe9ec0420b6
html:
I think authors will generally have many different views on what “internal” means, contrary to public.

Public is easy: it’s what I expose to users, and maintain to be free of breaking-changes.

Internal on the other hand can mean that the access at runtime is enforced or not, depending on a specific scope, whether bound to the language or how humans organize: same package, same module, same class, or same organization, same team, same project.

An example: you might want to completely prevent users from accessing an internal name, while allowing the same org uncomfortable access with a static analysis and runtime warning, while allowing the same team comfortable access with only a static analysis warning, while allowing the same project complete access without any warning. Or maybe something even finer grained, with package, module and class scopes.

What I mean is that maybe we should only standardize the public vs. internal declaration here (emphasis on public), and leave out what exactly “internal” means and implies. We’d drop questions 1 and 4.

The other option is of course to gather data around how projects handle and would like to handle internal APIs, and specify that too. But IMO there’s a clear cut and this can be done later.

A lot of my preference hinges on what happens to the existing methods. I’m quite sympathetic to wanting something better than import sys as _sys for single file modules.

But I also think the status quo for packages or using underscore-prefixed submoules and an __init__.py to export the public stuff trumps all these proposals, anything involving __all__, and anything I’ve used in other languages.

So anything that breaks that or even just insinuates that __all__ (or whatever else we come up with) is the preferred/official/correct/modern way to publicise an API gets an automatic -1 from me.

And yet, people can like one and hate the other - so how do we interpret their vote?

We interpret the vote only to the degree it is designed for: High-level approaches, not concrete solutions. Please do not expect that a handful of questions can cover the whole soution space for a topic as complex an nuanced as pubilc/internal. The poll does not aim to settle on a solution, it only structures and narrows the solution space. This limitation is intentional - It’s not a bug, it’s a feature.

We still can learn a lot:

Interpretation:
People do not want a global declatation (which the current__all__ pattern is).
Learning 1: There is a need beyond the status quo, so it’s worth to go into the topic.

Note that somewhere in the PEP 844 discussion there were voices advocating that having a single place at the top of the file declaring the public interface is actually benificial. That’s apparently a minority.
Learning 2: While being logically sound, the single place argument is not what people care about.
Learning 3: Concerning PEP 844, the local definition is a fundamentally desired property. It’s not just an incidental byproduct of improving management of __all__

author: e27a87eeed8d855855de38d3a3c16c3132984b80e6c50bca7824c454c6d50380
html:
While I agree that the poll is somewhat confusing, I’m in favor of the broader goal of figuring out what we want before getting into the weeds of individual PEPs. There are now three PEPs on this just in the span of a few weeks, and there is a good bit of crosstalk in the discussions comparing them to one another, and in a fair number of cases it appears that at least some people are rejecting fundamental goals or assumptions of one or more of them[1]. It seems to me that it would be better to hash out some of the underlying issues to hopefully come up with a proposal that has the broadest support, rather than just choosing among the existing proposals.

If I were going to make a poll it might be more like a yes/no (or in some cases multiple choice) thing on each of several questions, like (this is just off the top of my head):

  1. Should anything be changed from the status quo (aka “is there any problem that needs to be solved”)?
  2. Should Python gain a mechanism to in any way modify or enforce access control of things in modules/packages?
    a. If so, do we need more than two levels of access (i.e., is it enough to have just “public/private” or do we need something like “public only to other modules within the same package”)?
  3. Should Python gain a way to explicitly specify in a structured/machine-readable way what “the public API” of a module/package is, so that tools like IDEs can read this info?
  4. Whatever it is you think Python needs, is it sufficiently important to warrant adding some notes to the docs/a builtin function/a soft keyword/a hard keyword?

I get the impression there is substantial disagreement even on these basic issues, and in that situation I think it’s best to make no changes for the moment, and see if we can come up with something that has more support.

  1. e.g., disagreements about whether any change should be purely advisory/documentary or should have some effect on the semantics of imports or attribute access ↩︎
